points.text: Speaker F's minute-by-minute count shows overlaps in bursts throughout the meeting, not clustered in one region; this is not statistically verified.
The meeting had 215 overlaps in about 45 minutes, and only four minutes had none.
Speaker F says most overlaps in this meeting are benevolent types, such as backchannels, early answers and finishing each other's sentences, not hostile ones.
Speaker E's threshold-and-median-filter speaker detector works for one speaker but needs retuning for others, and the acoustic change detector performs poorly on close-talking mikes.
Audio pixelization replaces sensitive speech with a beep, applied on all channels and preserving timing; Speaker E has kept the original recordings.
Speaker E will add seat numbers to the enrollment forms so speaker positions are known.
Speaker E will send Speaker B a more specific sentence describing the digits-support work for the IBM list.
Speaker B asks everyone to send agenda ideas before the next meeting.
Speaker B asks participants to send corrections or additions to the three-month activity list for IBM.
Whether overlap rates depend on the number of people, compared with two-person conversations like Switchboard, is unresolved.
Speaker A and Speaker F disagree on whether two-person meetings serve as a control; Speaker A would record them but not as a priority.
A blindfold or no-visual-contact meeting is proposed, but the human subjects form would need work and Speaker B suggests waiting until the mikes are set up.
The group met to hear Speaker F's overlap analysis and Speaker E's speaker-detection work, and to review a three-month activity list for IBM.
The discussion was lively and ended with the group reading digits.
Speaker F counted overlaps per minute and by speaker pair; overlaps come in bursts, and Speaker E notes the raw counts need normalizing by how much each person speaks.
Speaker A asks how overlaps compare with two-person conversations, while Speaker B says the first-order finding is simply how many overlaps occur.
Speaker H proposes labeling overlaps as benevolent or competitive; Speaker B and Speaker F think most are competitive or benevolent rather than hostile.
Speaker E's energy-threshold detector is speaker-sensitive, and Javier's acoustic change detector performs poorly on close-talking mikes.
Speaker C suggests running a BIC change detector on all frames instead of relying on silence candidates.
Audio pixelization beeps out sensitive speech on all channels, keeping the timing intact.
Speaker F plans to subdivide the overlaps further and look at backchannels, hoping to report next time.

Participants are asked to send agenda ideas ahead of the next meeting.
Speaker F wrote a script that splits overlap markings into minutes and counts two-, three- and more-speaker overlaps, producing a table for the 45-minute meeting.
Speaker C has the duration of each overlap and plans to study their distribution.
Speaker E tried thresholding with median filtering, which works on one speaker with tuning, and implemented Javier's change detector on close-talking mikes.
Speaker E's audio pixelization software is written; Speaker B lists the XML formats, pilot data and release forms as done, with the next IBM batch still being prepared.
The threshold detector needs per-speaker tuning of filter width and threshold, even with loudness normalization.
The broad phone classifier in the change detector performs badly even on close-talking mikes.
Speaker E says the detector fails when the mike is worn on a lapel or far from the face.
The overlap counts are from one meeting with no statistical testing, so they cannot support firm findings.
